analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals, insurers, doctors, pharmacies, and drug makers to publicly post all prices they charge.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing or a vote, so health care prices remained undisclosed.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every health care provider, pharmacy, drug maker, and insurer to publish all prices for their products and services — including wholesale, retail, and discounted prices — both at the point of purchase and online, and let the Department of Health and Human Services fine companies that refused. It went to three House committees and none of them ever acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone paying for or shopping for health care, including uninsured patients who face sticker prices directly and employers who buy coverage. Publicly posted prices — including the discounted rates insurers actually negotiate — would let people compare costs before treatment, expose the gap between list prices and real prices, and create pressure on hospitals and drug makers to lower or simplify pricing.

how_it_helps.text: Requires any provider of health care products or services sold to the public — hospitals, doctors, pharmacies, drug makers, dentists, insurers — to disclose all prices continuously, at the point of purchase, in print, and on the internet.
Requires disclosure of every price accepted as payment in full, including wholesale, retail, subsidized, and discounted prices, so patients could see the actual rates, not just list prices.
Authorizes HHS to investigate noncompliance and impose civil fines or other penalties.
Applies the same disclosure duty to insurers and even to government programs administering Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and the federal employees' health plan.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, insurers, drug makers, doctors, dentists, and pharmacies, which would have had to publish and continuously update all prices and could face civil fines from HHS for noncompliance. Industry groups argued that revealing negotiated rates could raise some prices and impose heavy compliance costs.

drawbacks.text: Complying with continuous disclosure of every wholesale, retail, and discounted price would impose significant administrative costs on hospitals, physician practices, and pharmacies, especially small providers.

Publishing all prices accepted as payment in full, including discounted rates, could expose confidential negotiated rates and lead providers to raise their lowest discounted prices toward the published rates — a commonly argued risk of price-transparency rules — leaving some patients no better off.
Enforcement depends entirely on civil penalties that HHS 'may' impose, with no deadline or mandated penalty schedule, so an administration could decline to enforce the rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — real, comparable prices before treatment — is substantial and the main cost is a compliance burden on providers and insurers, plus the risk that negotiated discounts for big groups get published and pulled upward. The bigger design weakness is that transparency alone doesn't cap prices; disclosure helps only if patients can act on it, which is hard for emergency and specialist care.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and referred to the Health Subcommittee, and no committee ever acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced February 27, 2019 by Rep. Ed Perlmutter with nine cosponsors, including both Republicans and Democrats.
The House referred it to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Oversight and Reform — and to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
No committee reported the bill, no markup or hearing is recorded, and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended January 3, 2021.

The bill would have required public disclosure of all health care prices — wholesale, retail, and discounted — at the point of purchase and online, with HHS able to impose civil penalties for noncompliance.
Separate, narrower federal price-transparency rules for hospitals were issued by the Trump administration in 2019, but that action is not this bill; this bill died without any vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, insurers, and drug makers kept confidential pricing; patients and employers stayed without a full view of what care actually costs.

for.name: Ed Perlmutter
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Oversight committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled hearings or markups on the bill after it was referred to their committees, leaving it without any recorded action.

against.name: Hospital and insurer industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed broad disclosure of negotiated rates as trade secrets in the era's price-transparency debates.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Democrat and cosponsors included Republicans and Democrats, so the bill had bipartisan sponsorship but no vote ever occurred.

industries.note: Would have to publish every price they accept, exposing the wide gap between sticker prices and what insurers and uninsured shoppers actually pay. Hospitals have argued negotiated rates are trade secrets and have resisted disclosure.

Would have to disclose all prices for coverage and services, limiting their ability to negotiate confidentially and price discriminate. Their interest in keeping rates secret runs against patients who want to compare costs.
Would have to post all wholesale, retail, and discounted drug prices publicly. Disclosure alone does not cap prices, but it removes the information asymmetry drug makers rely on.
Bears the same disclosure duties as large institutions, which is a heavier relative burden on small practices, though published prices could also help small providers compete.
